missions/jesuit-asia-mission/name: Jesuits in Asia (Xavier, Valignano, Ricci, de Nobili, Japan, Chinese Rites)
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/statusNote: The original Jesuit Asian mission ended with the papal suppression of the Society in 1773, after the Chinese and Malabar rites had been condemned (1715, 1742, 1744) and Christianity proscribed in China (1724) and Japan (1614). The restored Society (1814) returned to Asia under very different conditions, and Rome effectively reversed the rites condemnation in 1939, so the Jesuits' policy of accommodation now shapes Catholic thinking on inculturation.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/summary: From Francis Xavier's landing at Goa in 1542 to the suppression of 1773, the Society of Jesus led Catholic mission in Asia under the Portuguese Padroado. Xavier baptised fishing castes in South India and opened Japan; Alessandro Valignano made cultural accommodation official policy; Matteo Ricci won a place at the Ming court as a Confucian-style scholar; Roberto de Nobili lived as a Brahmin sannyasi in Madurai. Japan's Christian community, perhaps 300,000 strong around 1600, was crushed after 1614. In China accommodation of ancestral and Confucian rites became the century-long Chinese Rites controversy, condemned by Rome in 1715 and 1742 and followed by imperial proscription; the Society itself was suppressed in 1773.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/story:
The Society of Jesus, approved by Paul III in 1540, was missionary from its foundation, and its members vowed special obedience to the pope regarding missions. At the request of King João III of Portugal, Francis Xavier sailed from Lisbon in April 1541 and reached Goa in May 1542 as papal nuncio. He worked first among the Paravars of the Fishery Coast, a fishing caste who had accepted mass baptism in 1535–37 in return for Portuguese protection against Muslim traders, and then among the Mukkuvas of Travancore, teaching prayers by rote in Tamil translation and baptising, by his own reports, many thousands. He travelled to Malacca, the Moluccas and, after meeting the Japanese fugitive Anjirō at Malacca, to Kagoshima in 1549. Xavier also wrote to João III in 1546 urging that an Inquisition be established in Goa, which was done in 1560. He died on Shangchuan Island off the Chinese coast in December 1552, waiting for passage into China.

Japan became the Jesuits' most spectacular field. Xavier learned that poverty did not impress Japanese elites and adopted fine dress and gifts to win audiences with daimyo. His successors gained the support of lords who wanted Portuguese trade: Ōmura Sumitada became the first Christian daimyo in 1563 and in 1580 ceded Nagasaki to the Society. Alessandro Valignano, visitor of the Asian missions from 1573, insisted that Jesuits learn Japanese etiquette and language, founded seminaries and a college, began training Japanese clergy and sent four young Japanese nobles to Lisbon, Madrid and Rome (the Tenshō embassy, 1582–90). By about 1600 there were perhaps 300,000 Christians. The darker side was real: Christian daimyo such as Ōmura and Arima ordered the destruction of Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines and pressed their vassals and subjects to convert; the Jesuits shared in the profits of the Macau–Nagasaki silk trade; and Portuguese merchants bought Japanese as slaves. In 1587 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, alarmed by Nagasaki's foreign control and by the Jesuit vice-provincial Gaspar Coelho's offers of Portuguese military help, issued an edict expelling missionaries. Rivalry with Spanish Franciscans from Manila, and the San Felipe incident, led to the crucifixion of twenty-six Christians at Nagasaki in 1597. The Tokugawa ban of 1614 began systematic persecution: thousands were executed, many after torture, apostates were registered at Buddhist temples and made to trample images (fumie), and the Shimabara rebellion of 1637–38 ended in massacre. Hidden Christians (Kakure Kirishitan) kept a transformed faith in secret for over two centuries.

In China Valignano sent Michele Ruggieri and Matteo Ricci, who settled at Zhaoqing in 1583. Ricci first wore Buddhist robes, then in 1595 adopted the dress of a Confucian scholar, and presented Christianity as the fulfilment of original Confucianism, criticising Buddhism and Neo-Confucian metaphysics. His world map, his treatises on friendship and memory, his translation with Xu Guangqi of Euclid's Elements (1607) and his catechism Tianzhu shiyi (The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven, 1603) won him admission to Beijing in 1601, where he lived on an imperial stipend until his death in 1610. Converts included the scholar-officials Xu Guangqi, Li Zhizao and Yang Tingyun. After the Ming fell, Johann Adam Schall von Bell directed the Qing Bureau of Astronomy; he was condemned to death in the calendar case of 1664–65 (commuted), but Ferdinand Verbiest restored the Jesuits' position, and the Kangxi Emperor issued an edict of toleration in 1692. Catholics numbered perhaps 200,000 by 1700, many of them in rural communities sustained by Chinese catechists and lay associations rather than by the court.

Ricci had allowed converts to continue honouring ancestors and Confucius, judging these civil rather than religious rites, and used classical terms such as Tian (Heaven) and Shangdi (Lord on High) for God. Spanish Dominicans and Franciscans arriving from Manila, notably Juan Bautista Morales, saw idolatry and appealed to Rome; the Propaganda condemned the practices in 1645, Alexander VII permitted them in 1656 on the Jesuit Martino Martini's representation, and the dispute escalated when the vicar apostolic Charles Maigrot banned the rites in Fujian in 1693. The Jesuits obtained a declaration from Kangxi in 1700 that the rites were civil, which Rome regarded as interference. Clement XI condemned the rites in 1704 and sent the legate Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon, whose audiences with Kangxi went badly; Tournon was expelled and died under Portuguese detention in Macau in 1710. The bull Ex illa die (1715) required all missionaries to swear obedience to the ban; Kangxi, reading it, remarked that Westerners could not understand Chinese teaching and it would be better to forbid their preaching. The Yongzheng Emperor proscribed Christianity in 1724, and Benedict XIV's Ex quo singulari (1742) closed debate. Christianity survived in China under persecution, but the opportunity of a court-sanctioned church had passed. In 1939 Pius XII's instruction Plane compertum est permitted Catholics to take part in ceremonies honouring Confucius and ancestors.

In India the Jesuits worked within the Padroado's Latin, Portuguese-speaking church, which was also suppressing the East Syriac heritage of the Thomas Christians; the Jesuit Francisco Ros became their first Latin bishop in 1601 after the Synod of Diamper. Roberto de Nobili, arriving in Madurai in 1606, separated himself from the Portuguese and the low-caste Paravar converts, lived as a vegetarian sannyasi, studied Sanskrit and Tamil, and argued that the sacred thread and caste marks were social signs that Brahmin converts could keep; Gregory XV approved his method in 1623. The Madurai mission later employed 'Brahmin sannyasis' for high castes and 'pandaraswamis' for others, with separate arrangements for Dalits – an accommodation of caste that the Malabar rites decrees of 1704 and 1744 (Omnium sollicitudinum) partly condemned and that left a legacy of segregated Catholic congregations. Jesuits also attended Akbar's court (from 1580), reached Tibet (Tsaparang 1624; Ippolito Desideri in Lhasa 1716–21), and in Vietnam Alexandre de Rhodes helped devise the romanised Vietnamese script (quốc ngữ) and published a catechism in 1651. In Ethiopia Jesuits from Goa secured the conversion of Emperor Susenyos in 1622, but the Latinising policy of Patriarch Afonso Mendes provoked civil war and expulsion in 1633.

European politics ended the mission. Pombal expelled the Jesuits from Portugal and its empire in 1759, France suppressed them in 1764 and Spain in 1767, and under Bourbon pressure Clement XIV dissolved the Society with Dominus ac Redemptor in 1773. Hundreds of Jesuits were shipped home from Asian and American missions; in Beijing the ex-Jesuits continued at court until the Lazarists took over in 1785. Pius VII restored the Society in 1814. Historians now regard the Jesuit Asian mission as both a remarkable intellectual bridge between Europe and Asia and a cautionary case of the costs of elite strategies, colonial entanglement and intra-Catholic rivalry.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/beliefs/0: Post-Tridentine Catholic orthodoxy with a strong emphasis on obedience to the pope and on the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/beliefs/1: Natural theology: reason and the best of non-Christian traditions (especially Confucian ethics) could prepare the way for revelation.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/beliefs/2: Accommodation (accommodatio): adopting local language, dress, etiquette and permissible customs while preserving doctrine.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/beliefs/3: Conversion of elites – rulers, daimyo, literati, Brahmins – as the key to reaching whole societies.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/beliefs/4: The distinction between civil and religious rites, applied to ancestral and Confucian ceremonies and to caste markers.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/strategies/: Rigorous language study and residence on local terms (Ricci's scholar's robes, de Nobili's sannyasi life).
Science, mathematics, astronomy, cartography and clockwork used to win access to courts.
Christian literature in Chinese, Japanese, Tamil and Vietnamese, including catechisms and apologetics.
Seminaries, colleges and printing presses (the Jesuit mission press in Japan from 1590).
Training of local catechists (dōjuku in Japan) and lay confraternities to sustain communities without priests.
Alliance with the Portuguese crown and trade networks for transport, funding and protection.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/groupsReach: Paravar and Mukkuva fishing communities of the Coromandel and Malabar coasts.
Japanese daimyo, samurai and peasants in Kyushu and central Japan.
Chinese scholar-officials and the Ming and Qing courts, and rural communities in Fujian, Jiangnan and Shanxi.
Brahmins and other castes of the Madurai region of Tamil Nadu.
The Mughal court of Akbar and Jahangir, without lasting conversions.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/challenges/: Persecution by Japanese and Chinese rulers who saw Christianity as foreign and subversive.
Rivalry with Spanish Franciscans and Dominicans and with the French priests of the Missions Étrangères de Paris.
Conflict between the Portuguese Padroado and Rome's vicars apostolic over jurisdiction.
Theological suspicion in Europe that accommodation compromised the faith, culminating in the Rites condemnations.
Few missionaries for vast populations, and long, deadly sea voyages.
The anti-Jesuit politics of Catholic Europe leading to expulsion and suppression.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/harms/0: Christian daimyo, with Jesuit approval, destroyed Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines and pressured subjects to convert; Buddhist monks were expelled from Christian domains.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/harms/1: Jesuits were entangled with Portuguese commerce, profited from the Macau–Nagasaki silk trade, and failed to stop Portuguese slave-trading in Japanese, which Hideyoshi cited in 1587.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/harms/2: Some Jesuits courted military intervention: Gaspar Coelho offered Hideyoshi Portuguese ships and fortified Nagasaki, and Alonso Sánchez proposed a Spanish conquest of China in the 1580s.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/harms/3: Xavier requested an Inquisition for Goa, which from 1560 prosecuted converts suspected of Hindu, Muslim or Jewish practices.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/harms/4: Mass baptisms of Paravars and Mukkuvas with minimal instruction made conversion a matter of caste politics and Portuguese patronage.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/harms/5: Caste accommodation in Madurai institutionalised discrimination against Dalit Christians, including separate seating, churches and priests.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/harms/6: The Rites controversy – a quarrel among European orders – left Chinese Catholics caught between Rome and the emperor and helped provoke the 1724 proscription.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/development: The most sustained intellectual exchange between Europe and East Asia before the nineteenth century, including Western mathematics in China and European knowledge of Confucianism.
Pioneering dictionaries and grammars (the Portuguese-Japanese Vocabulario of 1603, Ricci's romanisation, de Rhodes's Vietnamese dictionary).
The quốc ngữ script, now the standard written form of Vietnamese.
Durable Catholic communities in Tamil Nadu, Vietnam, China and Kyushu, including Japan's Hidden Christians.
A theology of inculturation later endorsed by Vatican II and by the 1939 reversal on Chinese rites.
A native Japanese clergy and the Japanese martyrs, honoured in Nagasaki's Christian heritage (UNESCO, 2018).
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/outcome: The Jesuits failed to convert the courts of Japan, China or Mughal India, and their Asian mission ended in proscription, persecution and the suppression of the Society; yet they left Catholic communities that survived without missionaries, a corpus of cross-cultural scholarship and a model of accommodation whose questions – how far Christianity may adopt local rites, castes and concepts – remain central to mission.

missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/0: Goa as base; Xavier on the Fishery Coast; de Nobili in Madurai; the Mughal court; Jesuit bishops of the Thomas Christians.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/1: Portuguese Malacca, where Xavier met Anjirō; a Jesuit college and hub for Asia.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/2: Xavier's mission on Ambon, Ternate and the Moro islands.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/3: From Kagoshima to about 300,000 Christians by 1600; persecution after 1614.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/4: Ricci and successors at Zhaoqing, Nanjing and Beijing; astronomers at the Qing court.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/5: Jesuit residence and, from 1594, the College of St Paul, training missionaries for China and Japan.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/6: Jesuits at Hội An and Tonkin; de Rhodes's catechism and romanised script.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/7: Jesuits joined the friar missions in Manila and the Visayas.

missions/jesuit-asia-mission/countries/9: Jesuits from Goa; Pedro Páez and the conversion of Susenyos; expulsion in 1633.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/journeys/0/: Francis Xavier, Paulo Camerte and Francisco Mansilhas
A thirteen-month voyage, including a winter on Mozambique Island, ended at Goa on 6 May 1542.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/journeys/1/: Xavier from India to the Moluccas and Japan
Francis Xavier, Cosme de Torres, Juan Fernández and Anjirō
Xavier's travels took him from the Pearl Fishery to the Spice Islands and to Japan, where he failed to see the emperor in Kyoto but founded communities at Yamaguchi and Bungo.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/journeys/2/: Francis Xavier and the Chinese servant Antonio
Waiting for a smuggler to take him to Canton, Xavier died of fever on Shangchuan on 3 December 1552.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/journeys/3/: Matteo Ricci, Michele Ruggieri and Lazzaro Cattaneo
Eighteen years of slow advance northward, changing from Buddhist to Confucian dress and building networks of literati friends, ended with residence at the Wanli court.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/journeys/4/: The Tenshō embassy of Japanese Christian youths
Itō Mancio, Chijiwa Miguel, Hara Martinho and Nakaura Julião with Diogo de Mesquita

Organised by Valignano to show Europe the Japanese church and Japan the glory of Catholic Europe; the youths met Philip II and Popes Gregory XIII and Sixtus V but returned to a country where Christianity had just been banned.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/journeys/5/: After learning Tamil on the Fishery Coast, de Nobili moved to Madurai in November 1606 and adopted the life of a sannyasi.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/relations/0: Worked under the Portuguese Padroado, depending on its ships, finances and enclaves (Goa, Malacca, Macau, Nagasaki).
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/agreements/: Jesuits used the Xi'an stele, rediscovered c. 1625, to show that Christianity had been honoured in China under the Tang, and like the Jingjiao monks they expressed Christian teaching in Chinese religious vocabulary.
Hudson Taylor's adoption of Chinese dress and residence among the people echoed Ricci's identification with Chinese culture, though for opposite social classes.
Ziegenbalg in Tranquebar, like the Jesuits of Madurai, studied Tamil literature seriously and tolerated caste distinctions in worship to a degree later Protestant missions condemned.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/disagreemen: Spanish Dominicans and Franciscans from Manila attacked Jesuit accommodation of ancestral rites and Confucian terms, taking the Chinese Rites controversy to Rome in 1643.
Jesuit attempts to Latinise the Ethiopian church under Susenyos provoked civil war and the expulsion of 1633.
De Nobili's caste-specific approach anticipated McGavran's 'homogeneous unit principle', which critics in both cases accused of entrenching caste.
missions/jesuit-asia-mission/deviations/: Ignatius's ideal of apostolic poverty and obedience coexisted with Jesuit trading ventures, estates and dependence on Portuguese colonial power.
Accommodation, designed to separate the gospel from European culture, was undermined by the Jesuits' own links to Portuguese empire and by Rome's ultimate rejection of the rites.
Concentration on elites left communities vulnerable when rulers turned hostile, as in Japan after 1587 and China after 1724.
Caste accommodation in Madurai departed from the wider Christian teaching of equality at the Lord's table.
